42949742|en.short: LEAP-Block was a randomized, multicenter superiority trial at 14 Chinese hospitals in 499 patients with atrioventricular block and LVEF ≥50%, comparing LBBAP with RVP. The 24-month composite of all-cause death, HF events, or biventricular pacing upgrade occurred in 2.4% vs 12.5% (P = .003). The authors conclude that LBBAP was superior to RVP.
42949742|en.headline: LBBAP vs RVP at 24 months: composite of death, HF events or biventricular upgrade 2.4% vs 12.5%
42949742|en.why_it_matters: The LEAP-Block trial randomized patients with atrioventricular block and preserved LVEF (≥50%) to left bundle-branch area pacing (LBBAP) or right ventricular pacing (RVP) and compared 24-month clinical outcomes. According to the abstract, the optimal pacing strategy to reduce heart failure and all-cause mortality in patients requiring high-burden ventricular pacing remains uncertain, and robust comparative evidence is needed.
42949742|en.key_finding: Of 499 randomized patients, 482 entered the primary analysis (LBBAP n = 242; RVP n = 240; mean age 67 years; 46% female). The primary end point occurred in 2.4% with LBBAP vs 12.5% with RVP (absolute risk difference -10.1% [95% CI, -16.8% to -3.4%]; P = .003). HF events were 3.4% vs 11.3% (-7.9% [95% CI, -13.0% to -2.8%]). The 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimated cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 5.0% vs 13.2% (hazard ratio, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.73]; P = .004). Acute procedure success was 97.9% vs 99.6% (P = .22). No significant differences were observed in all-cause death, biventricular pacing upgrade, device-related complications, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.

42949742|en.summary: The abstract states that the optimal pacing strategy to reduce heart failure (HF) and all-cause mortality in patients with atrioventricular block requiring high-burden ventricular pacing remains uncertain. LEAP-Block was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled, superiority trial conducted across 14 Chinese hospitals from January 2021 to August 2025, with last follow-up on June 3, 2025. Of 551 patients with LVEF 50% or greater requiring ventricular pacing who underwent eligibility assessment, 499 with anticipated ventricular pacing greater than 40% were randomized 1:1 to LBBAP (n = 249) or RVP (n = 250). The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months; secondary end points included pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and device-related complications. The primary analysis included 482 patients (LBBAP, n = 242; RVP, n = 240; mean age, 67 years; 46% female). Acute procedure success was 237/242 (97.9%) with LBBAP vs 239/240 (99.6%) with RVP (P = .22), and left bundle-branch capture was confirmed in 188 of 236 patients (79.7%). The primary end point occurred in 2.4% with LBBAP vs 12.5% with RVP (absolute risk difference, -10.1% [95% CI, -16.8% to -3.4%]; P = .003). HF events occurred in 3.4% vs 11.3% (-7.9% [95% CI, -13.0% to -2.8%]). No significant differences were observed in all-cause death, biventricular pacing upgrade, device-related complications, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimated cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 5.0% for LBBAP vs 13.2% for RVP (hazard ratio, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.73]; P = .004), and superiority of LBBAP was consistent across all prespecified subgroups. The authors conclude that LBBAP was superior to RVP in reducing the risk of the composite end point at 24 months.
42949742|en.relation_evidence: Right ventricular pacing is broadly known to be associated with pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and heart failure, and LBBAP is a conduction system pacing approach aimed at more physiological ventricular activation. This trial compares the two strategies using clinical outcomes in patients with preserved LVEF.
42949742|en.relation_guidelines: No clear guideline link can be derived.
42949742|en.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that, among patients with atrioventricular block and preserved LVEF requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, LBBAP was superior to RVP in reducing the risk of the composite of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months.

42956796|en.short: This individual participant data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (110 933 patient presentations) compared 0/1 h and 0/3 h pathways in suspected myocardial infarction. All-cause death or new type 1 MI within 30 days occurred in 0·8% versus 1·0% (pooled OR 0·83, 95% CI 0·45-1·53). The authors conclude the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise.
42956796|en.headline: 0/1 h vs 0/3 h pathway: 30-day death or new type 1 MI 0·8% vs 1·0%, pooled OR 0·83 (95% CI 0·45-1·53)
42956796|en.design_tag: IPD meta-analysis of 5 RCTs · 110 933 patient presentations
42956796|en.why_it_matters: This systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis pooled all randomised trials comparing the 0/1 h pathway with the 0/3 h pathway (standard care) in patients with suspected myocardial infarction, using harmonised outcome definitions. According to the background, the 0/1 h pathway is recommended in current guidelines, but individual trials used different safety outcomes and efficacy outcomes were inconclusive or not assessed.
42956796|en.key_finding: Five randomised trials, all providing individual participant data, were included, comprising 110 933 patient presentations (55 489 with the 0/1 h pathway and 55 444 with the 0/3 h pathway). All-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction within 30 days occurred in 446 (0·8%) versus 562 (1·0%) patient presentations (pooled OR 0·83 [95% CI 0·45-1·53]; I2=62·9%; τ2=0·143). Emergency department length of stay was 314 min (IQR 211-481) versus 308 min (209-453) (pooled geometric mean ratio 1·03 [95% CI 0·85-1·25]; I2=99·2%). Direct discharge occurred in 67·0% versus 65·8% (pooled OR 1·31 [95% CI 0·79-2·16]; I2=97·8%).
42956796|en.summary: In patients with suspected myocardial infarction, the 0/1 h pathway is recommended in current guidelines for early risk stratification, but individual trials used different safety outcomes and efficacy outcomes were inconclusive or not assessed. This systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis searched PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from inception to July 6, 2026, for randomised trials comparing 0/1 h with 0/3 h pathways. Outcome definitions were harmonised and the primary analysis used a two-stage random-effects meta-analysis. After receipt of the individual participant data but before harmonisation or analysis, the primary safety outcome was refined to all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction within 30 days. The primary efficacy outcomes were emergency department length of stay and direct discharge from the emergency department. Five randomised trials were identified, all providing individual participant data, with 110 933 patient presentations (55 489 with the 0/1 h pathway and 55 444 with the 0/3 h pathway). The primary safety outcome occurred in 446 (0·8%) versus 562 (1·0%) patient presentations (pooled OR 0·83 [95% CI 0·45-1·53]; I2=62·9%; τ2=0·143). Emergency department length of stay was 314 min (IQR 211-481) versus 308 min (209-453), with a pooled geometric mean ratio of 1·03 (95% CI 0·85-1·25; I2=99·2%; τ2=0·024). Direct discharge occurred in 37 190 (67·0%) versus 36 485 (65·8%) patient presentations (pooled OR 1·31 [95% CI 0·79-2·16]; I2=97·8%; τ2=0·156). The definition of the primary safety outcome varied among trials, and in four trials emergency department length of stay was not reported for the whole analysis population. The authors conclude that short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise, that earlier troponin retesting on average did not reduce length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and that substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems.
42956796|en.relation_evidence: According to the abstract, individual trials of the 0/1 h pathway had used different safety outcomes, with efficacy outcomes inconclusive or not assessed; this analysis pools all randomised trials with harmonised definitions. Further placement in the wider evidence base cannot be derived from the abstract alone.
42956796|en.relation_guidelines: The abstract states that the 0/1 h pathway is recommended in current guidelines for early risk stratification. The pooled randomised data reported here, with an imprecise safety estimate and substantial heterogeneity in efficacy outcomes, are described by the authors in that context; no specific guideline class or level of evidence is stated.
42956796|en.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that, across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise, and that earlier troponin retesting did not on average reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge. They state that, for hospitals considering a transition from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, broader diagnostic and organisational considerations are relevant to implementation decisions.

42953942|en.short: In this post hoc analysis of the SMART-CHOICE 3 randomized trial (5,506 patients after completed DAPT following PCI), MACCE in higher-risk patients was 4.6% with clopidogrel versus 7.4% with aspirin (HR 0.67). No difference was seen in lower-risk patients. The authors conclude clopidogrel was associated with lower ischemic risk without increased bleeding.
42953942|en.headline: Higher atherothrombotic risk: MACCE 4.6% with clopidogrel vs 7.4% with aspirin (HR 0.67); no difference in lower risk
42953942|en.design_tag: Post hoc RCT analysis · SMART-CHOICE 3 · N = 5,506
42953942|en.why_it_matters: This post hoc analysis of the SMART-CHOICE 3 randomized trial compared clopidogrel with aspirin monotherapy in patients who completed dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI, stratified by atherothrombotic risk (TIMI Risk Score for Secondary Prevention and complex PCI). The background states that it was unclear whether treatment effects differ by overall atherothrombotic risk integrating clinical and angiographic factors.
42953942|en.key_finding: Of 5,506 patients, 4,486 (81.5%) were classified as higher risk and 1,020 (18.5%) as lower risk. Over a median 2.3 years, MACCE occurred in 6.1% of higher-risk versus 3.1% of lower-risk patients (HR 1.83 [95% CI 1.17-2.78]; P=0.007). In higher-risk patients, MACCE was 4.6% with clopidogrel versus 7.4% with aspirin (HR 0.67 [95% CI 0.50-0.89]; P=0.006). In lower-risk patients, it was 3.0% versus 3.2% (HR 1.03; P=0.945; interaction P=0.242). Bleeding (BARC type 2, 3, or 5) was similar between groups.

42953942|en.summary: The background notes that clopidogrel monotherapy has shown superior efficacy compared with aspirin after completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following PCI, but that it was unclear whether the effect differs by overall atherothrombotic risk integrating clinical and angiographic factors. This was a post hoc analysis of the randomized SMART-CHOICE 3 trial, which included patients who completed guideline-directed dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI. Atherothrombotic risk was defined using the TIMI Risk Score for Secondary Prevention and complex PCI. Patients with a score ≥3 or complex PCI were classified as higher risk, and those with a score <3 without complex PCI as lower risk. The comparison was clopidogrel versus aspirin monotherapy. The primary end point was MACCE (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke), and bleeding was defined as BARC type 2, 3, or 5. Among 5,506 patients, 4,486 (81.5%) were higher risk and 1,020 (18.5%) lower risk. Over a median 2.3 years, MACCE was higher in the higher-risk group (6.1% versus 3.1%; HR 1.83 [95% CI 1.17-2.78]; P=0.007). In higher-risk patients, clopidogrel reduced MACCE compared with aspirin (4.6% versus 7.4%; HR 0.67 [95% CI 0.50-0.89]; P=0.006), whereas lower-risk patients showed 3.0% versus 3.2% (HR 1.03; P=0.945; interaction P=0.242). Bleeding was similar between groups. The authors conclude that clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with lower ischemic risk than aspirin in higher-risk patients, without increased bleeding.
42953942|en.relation_evidence: The abstract's background states that clopidogrel monotherapy has shown superior efficacy compared with aspirin after completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following PCI. This analysis examines whether that effect varies by atherothrombotic risk profile.
42953942|en.relation_guidelines: No clear guideline link can be derived.
42953942|en.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that, after completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following PCI, clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with lower ischemic risk than aspirin in patients with higher atherothrombotic risk, without increased bleeding.
